title: Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs)
description: Stack neurons into Input, Hidden, and Output layers to break linear separation limits like the XOR problem.

slides.title: Overcoming the XOR Problem 🧩
slides.content:
# The Fall and Rise of Neural Networks

In 1969, Minsky and Papert proved that a single perceptron cannot learn the simple **XOR (exclusive OR)** logic gate, because XOR is not linearly separable:

```
  x2
   1 |   (0,1) [+]     (1,1) [-]
     | 
   0 |   (0,0) [-]     (1,0) [+]
     +---------------------------
         0              1     x1
```

No single straight line can separate the `[+]` points from the `[-]` points! The solution? **Hidden Layers**. Stacking an intermediate layer projects the inputs into a transformed space where XOR becomes linearly separable.

quizData.question: Why could a single-layer perceptron without hidden layers not solve the XOR function?

options.text: XOR cannot be separated by a single linear decision hyperplane
Perceptrons can only output negative numbers

quizData.explanation: A single linear boundary cannot partition the diagonally placed positive and negative points of XOR. At least one hidden layer is mathematically required.

slides.title: Universal Approximation Theorem 🌟
slides.content:
## Universal Approximation Theorem (Hornik, 1989)
A standard feedforward neural network with just **a single hidden layer** containing a finite number of non-linear neurons can approximate *any continuous function* on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to arbitrary precision!

While one very wide hidden layer is theoretically sufficient, in practice, **deep networks** (many layers) learn hierarchical representations much more efficiently with far fewer parameters.
